hero.title: Sheffield Quantum Integration Lab
hero.strapline: Taking diamond quantum sensors from the physics lab to the chip.
hero.about: SQIL asks whether atom-like defects in solids, such as nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond, can be controlled at scale with the tools of the semiconductor industry: photonic circuits and cavities, multi-layer microwave electronics, and robotic field control.

image.caption: A silicon-nitride photonic chip fabricated at IMEC (optical micrograph, acquired at 5× magnification). Waveguides like these route light to and from arrays of diamond quantum sensors. Scale bar: 200 µm.

headlineResult.heading: Headline result
headlineResult.text: With colleagues at the University of Bristol, in 2026 we reported an eight-sensor photonic-integrated NV array with simultaneous, independent readout, used to localise a microscale magnetic tip (Weng, Rarity, Balram & Smith, Nature Communications 17, 6185). Our goal, funded by an EPSRC Quantum Technologies Career Acceleration Fellowship, is to scale this to a 64-pixel array.

researchPage.intro: We put photonics and electronics front and centre: with useful applications in adding spins to photonic quantum computing and networks, but also for more near-term implications for high resolution quantum sensing.

sections.title: Photonic-integrated NV sensor arrays
sections.label: Flagship theme
sections.summary: Diamond NV sensors read out through on-chip silicon-nitride waveguides: an eight-sensor array demonstrated with Bristol colleagues, and a 64-pixel array as our target.
sections.body: We integrate nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre sensors in diamond with silicon-nitride photonic chips, so that light is routed to and from each sensor through on-chip waveguides instead of bulk microscope optics. With colleagues at the University of Bristol we demonstrated an eight-sensor array with simultaneous, independent readout, used to localise a microscale magnetic tip (Nature Communications, 2026). Our fellowship aims to scale this to a 64-pixel array. In Sheffield we have built a photonic chip rig that couples multi-channel fibre arrays to on-chip waveguides. See Opportunities for related PhD opportunities. We are also applying chip-integrated quantum sensors to track magnetically labelled microbes, in an ARIA-funded seed project with the Bates Lab.

image.caption: An eight-channel fibre array aligned to a photonic chip on the SQIL rig in Sheffield (photo).

sections.title: Cavity-enhanced diamond sensors
sections.summary: Bulk diamond inside silicon-nitride/silica Bragg-mirror cavities made in Sheffield's cleanroom, aiming to cut the laser power NV sensors need.
sections.body: We place bulk diamond inside planar optical cavities made from silicon-nitride/silica Bragg mirrors (DBRs), deposited by PECVD in Sheffield's cleanroom. The aim is to raise NV excitation efficiency so sensors need less laser power. This work is with RobQuant Ltd, and results are being prepared for publication.

image.alt: Distributed Bragg reflector sample in the PECVD chamber in Sheffield’s cleanroom
image.caption: A silicon-nitride/silica Bragg mirror (DBR) sample after PECVD deposition in Sheffield’s cleanroom (photo).

sections.title: Scalable control and readout
sections.summary: Electronics for operating many spin sensors at once, from crosstalk-mitigated microelectronic control to FPGA-based ODMR readout.
sections.body: Reading out many spin sensors at once needs electronics that scale. With colleagues at the University of Bristol, we reported crosstalk-mitigated microelectronic control of spins (Physical Review Applied, 2026). We also develop FPGA-based optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) control and readout, and NV thermometry with a traceable calibration chain.

sections.title: Robotic vector-field alignment
sections.label: Established capability
sections.summary: Custom-built robotics that align large vector fields for spin-based quantum sensors.
sections.body: Advancing quantum sensing by aligning large vector fields with custom-built robotics. We build large-scale confocal microscopes to automate the characterization of quantum devices.

image.caption: Illustration of robotic vector-field alignment for a spin-based quantum sensor (Advanced Science, 2024).

pi.name: Dr Joe A. Smith
pi.bio: Joe joined the University of Sheffield in 2025, where he holds a five-year £1.6M EPSRC Quantum Technologies Career Acceleration Fellowship and is Lecturer in Quantum Technologies in the School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering. He leads SQIL, focusing on scalable control of solid-state quantum defects.

items.label: PhD opportunity — EPSRC DLA funding competition
items.title: PhD opportunity: Photonics for the scale up of quantum sensors (S3.5-ELE-Smith)
items.type: EPSRC Doctoral Landscape Award funding competition, October 2027 entry
items.location: University of Sheffield, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering
items.description:
Help build towards a 64-pixel diamond quantum sensor array on silicon photonics. The project aims to deposit diamond lithographically in micron-scale regions to form a spin-based sensor array, and to route each pixel's signal through silicon photonic waveguides. It builds on an eight-sensor photonic-integrated array demonstrated with colleagues at the University of Bristol (Nature Communications, 2026). You will work across photonic device simulation and design, cleanroom nanofabrication, device testing and proof-of-principle quantum sensing experiments. The project is underpinned by a five-year £1.6M EPSRC Quantum Technologies Career Acceleration Fellowship.

Supervisors: Dr Joe A. Smith and Dr Kristian Groom.
Funding is awarded by competition. Successful awards cover full tuition fees and a maintenance stipend at the applicable UKRI rate for 3.5 years, plus a research grant. Most DLA studentships go to candidates who qualify for Home fee status; see the current eligibility guidance.

Please get in touch before applying. Applications go through the EPSRC DLA application form (select this project).
